title: Equity Securities
fullTitle: Types and Characteristics of Equity Securities

los.text: Describe the characteristics of equity securities.
Identify the basic features of common stock.
Recognize the different types of preferred stock.
Describe how incentive stock options differ from nonqualified stock options.
Contrast restricted stock and nonrestricted stock.
Identify the unique features of ADRs and the risks of investing in foreign securities.

concepts.explanation: A security is either an ownership stake (equity: common or preferred stock) or a debt stake (a bond, which is a loan to the issuer). Stockholders are owners; bondholders are creditors. Every stockholder, including a preferred stockholder, is an owner, never a creditor.
rules: Common stock = ownership + vote + residual claim.
Preferred stock = ownership with a fixed dividend and priority over common for dividends and in liquidation; normally no vote.
Bond = loan; interest is a contractual obligation, dividends are not.
exceptions: Preferred stock behaves like a bond in price (interest-rate sensitive) but is legally equity.
examples: 100 shares outstanding: owning 10 shares = 10% of the company.
misconceptions: Thinking preferred stockholders are creditors because the dividend is fixed. They are owners.

concepts.explanation: Common stock rewards owners two ways: capital appreciation (price rises) and dividends. Dividends are declared at the board's discretion and are never guaranteed. They may be paid in cash, additional stock, or property. Historically stock returns have exceeded inflation, which is why common stock is treated as an inflation hedge.
rules: A gain is unrealized until the stock is sold; it is taxed only when realized.
Dividend yield = annual dividend ÷ market price.
formulas: Dividend yield = annual dividend per share ÷ current market price
misconceptions: Dividends are owed if the company is profitable — they are not; the board decides.

concepts.explanation: A stock dividend pays extra shares instead of cash; the price per share drops so total value is unchanged, and it is not taxed when received (it lowers cost basis per share). A stock split exchanges new shares for old (e.g., 2-for-1: twice the shares, half the price). Neither changes the investor's total value.
rules: Stock dividend: more shares, same total value, lower basis per share, no tax until sold.
Split: like exchanging a $20 bill for two $10s.
formulas: New price ≈ old total value ÷ new share count
examples: 100 shares at $48 = $4,800. After a 20% stock dividend: 120 shares, price ≈ $40, still $4,800.
misconceptions: Believing a stock dividend or split makes the investor richer.

concepts.explanation: Common stockholders vote for the board of directors, may freely transfer their shares (via the SEC-registered transfer agent), receive audited annual financial statements, and usually have a preemptive right to keep their proportional ownership when new shares are issued. Preferred holders generally do not have preemptive rights or votes. To vote or receive a declared dividend you must be an owner of record on the record date.
rules: Preemptive rights: common yes, preferred no.
Voting: common yes, preferred (for exam purposes) no.
Record date determines who votes / gets the dividend.
exceptions: Shareholders do not get earnings information before the public — being an owner confers no inside-information rights.
misconceptions: Thinking both common and preferred get preemptive rights.

concepts.explanation: Stockholders (common and preferred) have limited liability: the most they can lose is what they invested; creditors cannot reach their personal assets. Shares are liquid and freely transferable (restricted stock is the exception). Risks of common stock: market risk (price falls), business risk (earnings fall, dividend cut), and lowest priority at dissolution — bonds and preferred are senior; common has only a residual claim.
rules: Reasons to own common: appreciation, dividend income, inflation hedge.
Risks: market risk, business risk, last in line at liquidation.
exceptions: Restricted stock cannot be freely resold until Rule 144 conditions are met.
examples: Invest $5,000; company fails; maximum loss is $5,000.
misconceptions: Confusing limited liability with a guarantee against loss — you can lose the whole investment, just not more.

concepts.explanation: Preferred pays a fixed dividend stated either in dollars ($6 preferred) or as a percentage of par ($100 par, 6% = $6). Common can never receive a dividend until preferred has been paid. Straight (noncumulative) preferred: a skipped dividend is lost forever. Cumulative preferred: skipped dividends accumulate as arrears and must be paid, along with the current dividend, before common gets anything. Cumulative is the most suitable preferred for an investor seeking steady income.
rules: Arrears + current preferred dividend before any common dividend.
Bond interest is always paid before any dividend.
exceptions: Dividends on preferred are still discretionary — the board can skip them; cumulative just means they are owed later.
examples: $2 cumulative preferred skips 4 years, then resumes: holders get $8 arrears + $2 current = $10 before common is paid.
misconceptions: Thinking cumulative preferred is paid before bond interest; bonds come first.

concepts.explanation: Callable: the issuer may buy the shares back at a stated price after a stated date, usually when rates fall — dividends stop at the call; investors are compensated with a call premium over par and a slightly higher dividend, but they bear reinvestment risk. Convertible: exchangeable for a fixed number of common shares; its price tracks the common, it carries a lower dividend, and the feature reduces interest-rate risk. Adjustable-rate: dividend floats with benchmark rates (T-bills, money markets), so the price stays stable — least appropriate for someone wanting fixed income. Features can be combined (cumulative + callable + convertible).
rules: Callable → reinvestment risk; compensated by premium call price and higher dividend.
Convertible → lower dividend, price moves with common.
Adjustable → stable price, fluctuating dividend.
exceptions: Adjustable-rate preferred is the one preferred whose dividend is not fixed.
examples: $100 par callable at $103: issuer pays $103 to redeem when rates drop.
misconceptions: Picking adjustable-rate preferred for an income-seeker — its payment varies.

concepts.explanation: Preferred is bought for fixed dividend income and a prior claim over common. Its price reacts to interest rates like a bond (interest-rate/money-rate risk), so it carries market risk, purchasing-power risk, and business risk (dividend cut, bankruptcy). It is perpetual — no maturity or scheduled redemption. When analyzing a preferred for an income investor, the single most important factor is the company's ability to keep paying the dividend. Par value ($10, $25, $100) does not matter because the dividend is a percentage of par.
rules: Most important analysis point: ability to sustain the dividend.
Preferred has no maturity date.
exceptions: Preferred is classed as fixed income for allocation purposes, yet it is legally equity.
misconceptions: Choosing 'par value' or 'voting power' as the income investor's main concern.

concepts.explanation: Employee stock options give the right to buy employer stock at a strike (grant/exercise) price for a stated period, usually after a vesting period. Nonqualified stock options (NSOs/NQSOs) are the more common type and may go to employees, directors, even vendors. At exercise, the bargain element (market price − strike) is taxed to the employee as ordinary wages (including payroll taxes) and deducted by the employer as salary expense. The employee's cost basis becomes strike price + the bargain element already taxed.
rules: NSO tax event = exercise; bargain element = ordinary income.
Employer gets a deduction equal to the bargain element.
exceptions: No nondiscrimination rules apply to stock option plans (unlike qualified retirement plans).
formulas: Bargain element = (FMV at exercise − strike) × shares
misconceptions: Treating NSO gains at exercise as capital gains.

concepts.explanation: Incentive stock options (ISOs) are for employees only. No income at grant and no regular tax at exercise; tax comes when the stock is sold. If the stock is held at least 2 years from grant AND at least 1 year from exercise, the whole profit is long-term capital gain; otherwise it is taxed like an NSO. Options must be exercised within 10 years. Catch: the bargain element at exercise is a preference item for the alternative minimum tax (AMT). The employer gets no deduction.
rules: Holding test: ≥2 years after grant and ≥1 year after exercise → long-term capital gain.
Bargain element at exercise = AMT preference item.
Maximum 10-year exercise window.
exceptions: Fail either holding period → ordinary income treatment like an NSO.
examples: Granted Jan 2012 at $25; exercised Jan 2013 at $40 (no regular tax, $15 AMT adjustment); sold 2015 at $60 → $35/share long-term gain.
misconceptions: Thinking ISO exercise is a taxable event for regular income tax — it is not, but it affects AMT.

concepts.explanation: Two exceptions to free transferability. Restricted stock is acquired in an unregistered sale (private placement); all holders must generally hold it 6 months before resale, and affiliates also face volume limits. Control stock is any stock owned by a control person (director, officer, large holder — assume 10% or more of voting stock — or an immediate family member living in the same home); what matters is who owns it, not how it was acquired. Control stock always has volume limits, and sales must be reported. Both are sold under SEC Rule 144 of the Securities Act of 1933 by filing Form 144 — and it is the seller who files.
rules: Restricted: 6-month holding period for everyone; volume limits for affiliates.
Control: volume limits always; defined by ownership (10%+ assumed) including same-household family.
Form 144 is filed by the person selling.
exceptions: Spouses are assumed to live together, so a spouse of a 10%+ owner is also a control person even with a small holding.
examples: Investor owns 15%, spouse owns 5%: both are control persons; if only the spouse sells, only the spouse files Form 144.
misconceptions: Thinking restricted stock requires a 1-year hold (it is 6 months) or that restrictions apply only to control persons.

concepts.explanation: An American depositary receipt (ADR, also ADS) is a negotiable receipt, issued by domestic branches of U.S. banks, representing shares of a non-U.S. company; it trades in U.S. markets in dollars and pays dividends in dollars. One ADR may equal one share, several shares, or a fraction of a share (the ratio makes the price look like a typical U.S. stock). ADR holders get dividends and sometimes votes, but never preemptive rights. The bank converts dividends to dollars and withholds any foreign tax; the holder can claim a U.S. tax credit for that withholding. Despite trading in dollars, ADRs still carry currency risk.
rules: Issued by U.S. banks; traded and paid in USD.
Never preemptive rights; voting sometimes.
Currency risk remains.
exceptions: Ratios other than 1:1 exist (concept tested, math not).
examples: A 1:5 ADR at $10 = five underlying shares worth about 55 Brazilian reals.
misconceptions: Assuming USD trading removes currency risk — it does not.

concepts.subtopic: Emerging vs. developed markets; foreign risks
concepts.explanation: Emerging markets: lower GDP and capitalization, questionable liquidity, currency-conversion limits, high volatility, high taxes and commissions, restrictions on foreign ownership, weaker regulation and transparency — but rapid growth prospects. (Frontier markets are riskier still.) Developed markets: large capitalization, low commissions, few currency restrictions, deep liquidity, strong regulation. Foreign securities expand diversification and are usually not highly correlated with U.S. securities, which lowers portfolio risk. Extra risks: country risk (political and structural, e.g., coups, confiscatory policies), exchange controls, currency risk, and withholding taxes and fees.
rules: Why go foreign: wider universe, possible outperformance, low correlation.
Four foreign-specific risks: country, exchange controls, currency, withholding/fees.
misconceptions: Confusing country risk (political/structural) with currency risk (exchange-rate movement).

lessons.title: Owners vs. lenders: what common stock gives you
lessons.objective: Explain why stockholders are owners, what common stock pays, how stock dividends and splits work, and the rights, protections, and risks of common ownership.

blocks.b:
Every security is either a slice of **ownership** (equity) or a **loan** (debt).
- Buy stock → you are an **owner**. Common and preferred stock are both equity.
- Buy a bond → you are a **creditor**. The issuer owes you interest and repayment at maturity.

The exam loves to test the line between the two: a preferred stockholder has a fixed dividend and looks bond-like, but is still an owner, never a creditor.

Owners of common stock can profit two ways:
- **Capital appreciation** — the share price rises. Until you sell, the gain is *unrealized* and untaxed.
- **Dividends** — cash, extra shares, or property paid at the **board's discretion**. Nothing obliges a company to pay a dividend, even in a profitable year.

Because stock returns have historically beaten inflation, common stock is treated as an **inflation hedge**.

**Dividend yield** = annual dividend ÷ market price. A $2 dividend on a $60 stock is a 3.33% yield.
You buy RST at $60 on Jan 1. It pays $2 in dividends during the year and closes Dec 31 at $90. Your dividend yield on cost is 3.33%, and you have a $30 unrealized gain — taxed only when you sell.

blocks.h: Stock dividends and splits change the count, not the value
blocks.b:
A **stock dividend** pays additional shares instead of cash. The price adjusts down so your total value is unchanged; it is **not taxed when received** and lowers your cost basis per share.

A **stock split** swaps old shares for new ones (2-for-1: twice the shares, each worth half). Think of breaking a $20 bill into two $10s — same money, more pieces.
100 shares at $48 = $4,800. A 20% stock dividend gives you 120 shares, so the price falls to about $40. Still $4,800.

blocks.h: Rights that come with common stock
blocks.b:
- **Vote** for the board of directors (one vote per share).
- **Transfer** shares freely — the SEC-registered **transfer agent** reissues the certificate in the buyer's name. No issuer permission needed.
- Receive **audited annual financial statements**.
- **Preemptive right** to buy enough of any new issue to keep your ownership percentage. **Common has it; preferred does not.**

To vote or collect a declared dividend you must be the owner on the company's books by the **record date**.

Being an owner does **not** give you early access to earnings or other inside information.

blocks.h: Limited liability, liquidity, and the risks
blocks.b:
**Limited liability**: if the company fails, you can lose everything you invested — but creditors can never come after your personal assets. (Contrast a sole proprietorship or general partnership, where personal assets are exposed.)

**Liquidity**: shares are freely transferable, especially exchange-listed ones. The exception is **restricted stock** (Lesson 1.3).

Why own common stock: appreciation, dividend income, inflation hedge.

Risks you take on:
- **Market risk** — the price can fall for any reason.
- **Business risk** — earnings decline, dividend cut or eliminated.
- **Low priority at dissolution** — bonds and preferred are *senior*; common holders get only what is left (a *residual* claim).

lessons.title: Preferred stock: the equity that acts like a bond
lessons.objective: Distinguish straight, cumulative, callable, convertible and adjustable-rate preferred; identify who gets paid first; and pick the right preferred for an income investor.

blocks.b:
Preferred stock is **equity** with a **fixed dividend**, stated either in dollars ("$6 preferred") or as a percent of par ("$100 par, 6%" = $6). The rule that gives it its name: **common can never receive a dividend until preferred has been paid.**

Because the payment is fixed, the price moves with **interest rates** like a bond, so advisers usually treat preferred as fixed income for allocation purposes. For the exam, preferred is **nonvoting** unless a question says otherwise, and it has **no maturity** — it is perpetual.

- **Straight (noncumulative)**: just the stated dividend. A skipped dividend is gone forever.
- **Cumulative**: skipped dividends pile up as **dividends in arrears**. When payments resume, the company must pay **all arrears plus the current dividend** before common gets a cent.

An investor who wants **steady income** should prefer **cumulative** — it is the most suitable type for that goal.

Order of payment never changes: **bond interest → preferred (arrears, then current) → common.**

RST's $2 cumulative preferred skipped 2017–2020. In 2021 the company resumes dividends: it must pay $8 of arrears plus the $2 current dividend ($10 total) to preferred before common receives anything.

**Callable (redeemable)** — the issuer can buy the shares back at a set price after a set date, typically when rates have fallen (like refinancing a mortgage). Dividends stop at the call. You are compensated with a **call premium** (e.g., $103 on $100 par) and a slightly **higher dividend**, but you face **reinvestment risk**.

**Convertible** — you may swap each preferred share for a fixed number of common shares. Its price tends to track the common, it pays a **lower dividend** (you are paying for upside), and the feature **reduces interest-rate risk**.

**Adjustable-rate (floating)** — the dividend resets to a benchmark such as T-bill rates, so the **price stays stable** while the **payment fluctuates**. For someone who wants fixed income this is the **least appropriate** preferred.

Features stack: a stock can be cumulative, callable *and* convertible. No adjectives = straight preferred.

blocks.h: Why buy it, what can go wrong, what to analyze
blocks.b:
Reasons: fixed dividend income; a claim **ahead of common**; convertible preferred trades some income for appreciation potential.

Risks: **market risk** (price drops if the dividend looks shaky), **purchasing-power risk**, **interest-rate (money-rate) risk**, and **business risk** up to bankruptcy.

When an income investor evaluates a specific preferred, the **most important** question is the company's **ability to keep paying the dividend**. Par value is irrelevant (the dividend is a percent of whatever par is), and voting power is irrelevant (there is none).

lessons.title: Employee stock options and stock you can't just sell
lessons.objective: Compare NSO and ISO taxation, and explain restricted stock, control stock, and Rule 144 / Form 144.

blocks.b:
An employee stock option is the right to buy employer stock at a **strike price** (also called grant or exercise price — usually the market price on the grant date) during a stated period, once a **vesting period** has passed. The employee hopes the market price rises above the strike. These plans have **no nondiscrimination rules** (unlike qualified retirement plans) and usually need board approval.

Two kinds, with very different tax results: **NSOs** and **ISOs**.

blocks.h: NSOs: taxed as wages at exercise
blocks.b:
**Nonqualified stock options** (NSOs/NQSOs) are the more common kind and can go to employees, directors, even vendors.

At **exercise**, the **bargain element** — market price minus strike — is **ordinary income** to the employee (subject to payroll taxes too) and a **salary-expense deduction** for the employer. The employee's cost basis in the shares = strike + the bargain element already taxed.
Susan exercises NSOs on 500 shares at a $20 strike when the stock is $30. Bargain element = $10 × 500 = $5,000 of ordinary income. At a 28% rate, that is $1,400 of income tax (plus payroll taxes).

blocks.h: ISOs: capital-gain treatment if you wait
blocks.b:
**Incentive stock options** are for **employees only**. The employer gets **no deduction**, but the employee can do much better:
- **Grant**: no income.
- **Exercise**: no regular income tax.
- **Sale**: profit is **long-term capital gain** — but only if the stock was held **at least 2 years after the grant AND at least 1 year after exercise**. Miss either and it is taxed like an NSO.
- Options must be exercised within **10 years**.

**The catch**: the bargain element at exercise is a **preference item for the alternative minimum tax (AMT)**. The exam mainly wants you to know ISOs *can* trigger AMT.

rows: Capital gain on growth after exercise
Long-term capital gain if 2-yr/1-yr holding met

blocks.b:
Stock is normally freely transferable. Two testable exceptions:

**Restricted stock** — acquired in an unregistered (private placement) sale. **Everyone** must hold it generally **6 months** before resale; **affiliates** also face **volume limits**.

**Control stock** — stock owned by a **control person**: a director, officer, large stockholder (assume **10% or more** of voting stock), or an **immediate family member living in the same home**. It is defined by *who owns it*, not how it was acquired. Control stock **always** has volume limits and sales are reported to the SEC.

Both are sold under **SEC Rule 144** (Securities Act of 1933) by filing **Form 144** — filed by **the seller**.
An investor owns 15% of a public company; the spouse (same home) owns 5%. Both are control persons. If only the spouse sells, only the spouse files Form 144.

lessons.title: ADRs and investing abroad
lessons.objective: Describe how ADRs work, what rights they carry, and the specific risks and characteristics of emerging vs. developed foreign markets.

blocks.b:
An **American depositary receipt** (ADR, also called an ADS) is a negotiable receipt for shares of a **non-U.S. company**, issued by **domestic branches of U.S. banks**. It trades in U.S. markets **in dollars**, and dividends arrive **in dollars** — everything in English and USD, which is the whole point.

One ADR can represent one share, several shares, or a fraction of a share; the ratio is chosen so the ADR trades at a typical U.S. price. The math is not tested, only that ratios other than 1:1 exist.

blocks.h: Rights and risks of ADR holders
blocks.b:
- **Dividends**: yes. The bank collects them, converts to dollars, and **withholds any foreign tax** — the holder can claim a **U.S. tax credit** for it.
- **Voting**: sometimes.
- **Preemptive rights**: **never** (for the exam).

Even though you pay and receive dollars, the underlying shares are priced in a foreign currency, so ADRs **still carry currency risk**. The two risks of greatest concern to an ADR holder are **currency risk and market risk**; ADRs on exchanges have little liquidity risk, and as equity they hedge purchasing-power risk.

**Emerging markets** (less-developed countries): low GDP and equity capitalization, questionable liquidity, currency-conversion restrictions, high volatility, high taxes and commissions, limits on foreign ownership, lower regulatory standards (less transparency) — offset by **rapid growth prospects** and stabilizing institutions. (**Frontier markets** are even riskier.)

**Developed markets**: large capitalization, low commissions, few currency restrictions, deep liquidity with many market makers, and transparent regulation similar to the U.S.

Why add foreign securities: a **bigger investment universe** (more diversification), they sometimes **outperform**, and they are **not highly correlated** with U.S. securities, which **lowers portfolio risk**.

blocks.h: Four risks unique to foreign investing
blocks.b:
- **Country risk** — the composite of political risk (coups, revolutions) and structural risk (confiscatory policies toward profits or dividends), plus the country's economic policies.
- **Exchange controls** — limits on converting or moving currency.
- **Currency risk** — the foreign currency weakens against the dollar.
- **Withholding taxes and fees** — taxes withheld on dividends/gains and higher commissions.

Keep *country* risk (politics/structure) separate from *currency* risk (exchange rates).

questions.stem: Which of the following investors is a creditor of the issuer?
options: An individual holding cumulative preferred stock of XYZ Corp.
A pension fund holding XYZ Corp. common stock
A mutual fund holding XYZ Corp. debentures
An employee holding exercised XYZ Corp. stock options
questions.explanation: A debenture is a bond — a loan to the issuer — so its holder is a creditor. Every form of stock, including preferred and shares acquired through options, represents ownership.
why: Preferred stock is equity; the fixed dividend does not make the holder a lender.
Common stock is ownership regardless of who holds it.
Exercised options become common shares — ownership.

questions.stem: Compared with common stock, preferred stock typically
options: carries greater voting power and greater appreciation potential.
pays a fixed dividend and has a prior claim on dividends and assets.
represents a loan to the corporation that matures on a stated date.
fluctuates in price mainly with the company's business prospects.
questions.explanation: Preferred stock normally pays a fixed dividend, is paid before common on dividends and in liquidation, usually has no vote, and its price responds mainly to interest rates.
why: Preferred usually has no vote and less appreciation potential.
Preferred is equity, not debt, and has no maturity.
That describes common stock; preferred reacts to interest rates like a bond.

questions.stem: An investor bought 200 shares of MNO at $40. During the year MNO paid quarterly dividends of $0.30 per share and the stock ended the year at $46. Which statement is correct?
options: The investor has a realized gain of $1,200 and a dividend yield of 3%.
The investor has an unrealized gain of $1,200 and a dividend yield on cost of 3%.
The investor has an unrealized gain of $1,200 and a dividend yield on cost of 0.75%.
The investor has taxable capital gain of $1,200 this year.
questions.explanation: Gain = ($46 − $40) × 200 = $1,200, unrealized because nothing was sold. Annual dividend = $0.30 × 4 = $1.20; $1.20 ÷ $40 = 3%.
why: The gain is unrealized — no sale occurred.
0.75% uses one quarterly dividend instead of the annual total.
Capital gains are taxed only when realized.

questions.stem: A corporation reports record profits for the year. Regarding dividends on its common stock, which statement is true?
options: Common stockholders are entitled to a dividend because the company was profitable.
A dividend may be paid only in cash.
Any dividend is paid at the discretion of the board of directors.
The dividend must at least equal the previous year's dividend.
questions.explanation: Dividends on equity are never obligatory; the board decides whether and how much to pay, in cash, stock, or property.
why: Profitability creates no entitlement.
Dividends can be cash, additional shares, or property.
There is no requirement to maintain or raise a dividend.

questions.stem: An investor owns 300 shares of ABC at $50 per share. ABC declares a 10% stock dividend. After the distribution, the investor most likely holds
options: 330 shares worth approximately $45.45 each, total value $15,000.
330 shares worth $50 each, total value $16,500.
300 shares worth $55 each, total value $16,500.
330 shares worth approximately $45.45 each, and owes tax on the 30 new shares.
questions.explanation: A stock dividend adds shares but no new money, so the price falls to keep total value constant: $15,000 ÷ 330 = $45.45. Stock dividends are not taxed when received.
why: The price must adjust downward; total value cannot rise from a stock dividend.
Share count rises, not the price.
Stock dividends are not taxable when received; they reduce cost basis per share.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a 3-for-1 stock split on an investor who owned 100 shares at $90?
options: 300 shares at $30; total value unchanged; no tax due.
300 shares at $90; total value triples.
100 shares at $30; total value falls by two-thirds.
300 shares at $30; the $60 per-share decline is a deductible loss.
questions.explanation: A split changes the number of shares and price proportionally — like changing a $20 bill for smaller bills — leaving total value unchanged and creating no taxable event.
why: Price falls proportionally; value does not change.
The share count triples.
No gain or loss is realized in a split.

questions.stem: GHI Corp. plans to issue additional common shares. Which of its security holders generally have the right to maintain their proportionate ownership by buying the new shares first?
options: Holders of GHI common stock only
Holders of GHI preferred stock only
Holders of both GHI common and preferred stock
Holders of GHI ADRs and common stock
questions.explanation: The preemptive right belongs to common stockholders. Preferred holders get dividend and liquidation preference instead, and ADRs never carry preemptive rights.
why: Preferred stock generally has no preemptive right.
Only common has it.
ADRs never carry preemptive rights for exam purposes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a right of a common stockholder?
options: Receiving audited annual financial statements
Voting for the board of directors
Access to quarterly earnings figures before they are released to the public
Transferring shares without the issuer's permission
questions.explanation: Owning stock gives no access to material nonpublic information. Audited statements, the vote, and free transferability are all stockholder rights.
why: This is a stockholder right.
This is a stockholder right.
Free transferability is fundamental to stock ownership.

questions.stem: A client invested $8,000 in the common stock of a corporation that has just filed for bankruptcy with liabilities far exceeding its assets. The client's maximum exposure is
options: $8,000 plus a proportional share of the unpaid corporate debts.
the amount of debt the creditors choose to pursue from shareholders.
unlimited, as with any business owner.
questions.explanation: Limited liability means a stockholder can lose no more than the amount invested; creditors cannot reach personal assets.
why: Shareholders do not absorb corporate debts.
Creditors have no claim on shareholders' personal assets.
Unlimited liability applies to sole proprietors and general partners, not stockholders.

questions.stem: All of the following are reasons an adviser might include common stock in a client's portfolio EXCEPT
options: potential capital appreciation.
a historical hedge against inflation.
dividend income.
priority over bondholders if the company is liquidated.
questions.explanation: Common stock has the lowest priority at dissolution — bonds and preferred stock are senior securities. Appreciation, inflation hedging, and dividends are the reasons to own common stock.
why: Appreciation is a core reason to own common stock.
Stocks have historically outpaced inflation.
Dividends are a major source of return.

questions.stem: XYZ has $4 cumulative preferred stock outstanding. It paid no dividends in 2024 or 2025. In 2026 the board wants to pay a common dividend. Before any common dividend, the preferred holders must receive
options: $4, the current year's dividend only.
$8, the two years in arrears only.
$12, the two years in arrears plus the current year.
nothing, because dividends are discretionary.
questions.explanation: Cumulative preferred accumulates missed dividends. Arrears ($4 × 2 = $8) plus the current $4 must be paid before common receives anything.
why: Arrears must be paid too.
The current dividend must also be paid first.
Dividends are discretionary, but once a common dividend is paid, the cumulative preferred must be satisfied first.

questions.stem: In what order must a corporation make the following payments?
options: Common dividends, preferred dividends, bond interest
Preferred dividends in arrears, bond interest, common dividends
Bond interest, preferred dividends in arrears and current, common dividends
Bond interest, common dividends, preferred dividends
questions.explanation: Interest on debt is a contractual obligation paid first. Then cumulative preferred arrears plus the current preferred dividend, and only then common.
why: Reversed — common is always last.
Bond interest always precedes any dividend.
Preferred must be paid before common.

questions.stem: A retired client wants the most dependable dividend stream available from a single issuer's preferred stock. Which type is most suitable?
options: Straight preferred
Cumulative preferred
Adjustable-rate preferred
Convertible preferred
questions.explanation: Cumulative preferred is the only type under which skipped dividends must later be made up before common is paid, making it the most suitable for steady income.
why: Missed straight-preferred dividends are lost.
The adjustable dividend fluctuates — least appropriate for fixed income.
Convertible pays a lower dividend in exchange for upside.

questions.stem: Interest rates have fallen sharply since a client bought a $100 par, 7% callable preferred. The issuer announces it will redeem the shares at $103. The client is now primarily exposed to
options: interest-rate risk.
reinvestment risk.
business risk.
currency risk.
questions.explanation: When a high-dividend preferred is called in a low-rate environment, the holder must reinvest the proceeds at lower rates — reinvestment risk. The premium call price partly compensates.
why: The call removes the price exposure; the problem is what to do with the cash.
A call reflects lower rates, not deteriorating business.
A domestic preferred has no currency risk.

questions.stem: Which statement about convertible preferred stock is correct?
options: It usually carries a higher dividend than nonconvertible preferred of the same quality.
Its market price tends to move with the price of the issuer's common stock.
It is the preferred most sensitive to interest-rate changes.
It can be exchanged for bonds of the issuer.
questions.explanation: Because it can be exchanged for a fixed number of common shares, convertible preferred's price tracks the common. The feature is paid for with a lower dividend and tends to reduce interest-rate risk.
why: Convertible preferred pays a lower dividend.
The conversion feature reduces interest-rate sensitivity.
Conversion is into common stock.

questions.stem: An investor whose sole objective is a fixed, predictable dividend would find which preferred stock LEAST appropriate?
options: Cumulative preferred
Callable preferred
Adjustable-rate preferred
Straight preferred
questions.explanation: An adjustable-rate preferred resets its dividend to benchmark interest rates, so the payment fluctuates — the opposite of fixed income.
why: Cumulative is the best choice for steady income.
Callable pays a fixed (slightly higher) dividend until called.
Straight preferred pays a fixed dividend.

questions.stem: An IAR is comparing two preferred stocks for a client whose objective is quarterly income. The most important factor to evaluate is
options: which issue has the higher par value.
which issue carries voting rights.
each issuer's ability to continue paying the stated dividend.
which issue has the earlier maturity date.
questions.explanation: For an income investor, the ability to sustain the dividend is paramount. Par value is irrelevant (dividend is a percent of par), preferred is nonvoting, and preferred has no maturity.
why: The dividend is a percentage of par, so par size does not matter.
Preferred stock is nonvoting for exam purposes.
Preferred is perpetual; it has no maturity date.

questions.stem: Which of the following risks is NOT typically associated with owning preferred stock?
options: Interest-rate (money-rate) risk
Purchasing-power risk
Risk of forced conversion into bonds at maturity
Business risk leading to a dividend cut
questions.explanation: Preferred stock has no maturity and is never converted into bonds. It does carry interest-rate, purchasing-power, market, and business risk.
why: Fixed dividend → price moves inversely with rates.
A fixed payment loses purchasing power to inflation.
Dividends can be reduced or eliminated.

questions.stem: An employee exercises nonqualified stock options on 400 shares at a $15 strike when the stock trades at $27. The employee's marginal income tax rate is 24%. The income tax on the exercise is
options: $0; no tax is due until the shares are sold.
$1,152, taxed as ordinary income.
$1,152, taxed as long-term capital gain.
$2,592, taxed as ordinary income.
questions.explanation: Bargain element = ($27 − $15) × 400 = $4,800, taxed as ordinary wages: $4,800 × 24% = $1,152.
why: NSO exercise is the taxable event.
NSO bargain element is ordinary income, never capital gain.
$2,592 taxes the full $27 value instead of the spread.

questions.stem: When an employee exercises a nonqualified stock option, the issuing corporation
options: recognizes a long-term capital gain.
receives a tax deduction equal to the bargain element.
has no tax consequence.
must withhold the bargain element as a preference item.
questions.explanation: The bargain element is treated as wages: ordinary income to the employee and a deductible salary expense to the employer.
why: The corporation has no capital gain on issuing its own shares.
No tax consequence to the employer describes an ISO, not an NSO.
AMT preference items relate to ISOs.

questions.stem: An employee was granted ISOs on March 1, 2023, exercised them on June 1, 2025, and sold the shares on March 15, 2026. The profit on the shares will be taxed as
options: long-term capital gain, because the shares were held more than one year after exercise.
long-term capital gain, because the sale is more than two years after the grant.
ordinary income, because the shares were sold less than one year after exercise.
ordinary income, because ISO profits are always wages.
questions.explanation: ISO capital-gain treatment requires BOTH at least 2 years from grant AND at least 1 year from exercise. The grant test is met (3 years), but the exercise-to-sale period is only about 9.5 months, so the ISO is taxed like an NSO.
why: Exercise to sale is under one year.
Both holding tests must be met, not just one.
ISO profits can be capital gain when both holding periods are satisfied.

questions.stem: Which statement about incentive stock options is correct?
options: The employer deducts the bargain element as salary expense.
The bargain element at exercise is a preference item for the alternative minimum tax.
They may be granted to vendors and outside directors.
The bargain element is taxed as ordinary income at exercise.
questions.explanation: ISOs give the employer no deduction, are for employees only, and create no regular tax at exercise — but the spread at exercise is an AMT preference item.
why: That describes NSOs.
ISOs are solely for employees.
No regular income tax is due at exercise of an ISO.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a difference between NSOs and ISOs?
options: Only ISOs require a vesting period.
Only NSOs can be exercised within 10 years of grant.
NSOs produce ordinary income at exercise; ISOs produce no regular income at exercise.
ISOs are subject to nondiscrimination rules; NSOs are not.
questions.explanation: The core tax difference: NSO exercise creates ordinary income on the bargain element; ISO exercise creates no regular income (though it affects AMT).
why: Both types commonly have vesting periods.
The 10-year limit is an ISO rule.
Neither type is subject to nondiscrimination requirements.

questions.stem:
Marcus owns 12% of the voting stock of a publicly traded company. His wife, who lives with him, owns 2% that she bought on the open market. If she sells her shares, which statements are TRUE?
I. She is a control person.
II. Her shares are restricted stock.
III. She must file Form 144.
IV. Marcus must file Form 144.
options: I and III
I and IV
II and III
II and IV
questions.explanation: Control is defined by ownership: 10%+ holders and immediate family in the same household are control persons, so her shares are control stock (not restricted — she bought them in the market). The seller files Form 144, and she is the one selling.
why: The person selling files the form; Marcus is not selling.
Open-market shares are not restricted; they are control stock because of who owns them.
Neither statement fits.

questions.stem: Which statement about restricted stock is correct?
options: It must be held at least one year before it may be resold.
It is subject to a holding period for all purchasers, and volume limits for affiliates.
Only control persons are subject to its restrictions.
Its sale is reported on Form U4.
questions.explanation: Restricted (private placement) stock carries a holding period — generally six months — for every holder; affiliates face volume limits as well. Sales are reported on Form 144.
why: The holding period is generally six months.
The holding period applies to all holders.
Form 144 is used; Form U4 is a registration form for industry personnel.

questions.stem: What distinguishes control stock from restricted stock?
options: Control stock is defined by how it was acquired; restricted stock by who owns it.
Control stock is defined by who owns it; restricted stock by how it was acquired.
Only restricted stock is sold under Rule 144.
Only control stock has a holding period.
questions.explanation: Control stock is any stock owned by a control person regardless of source; restricted stock is stock acquired in an unregistered transaction. Both are sold under Rule 144; the holding period applies to restricted stock.
why: Reversed.
Both are sold under Rule 144 using Form 144.
The holding period is a restricted-stock feature; control stock has volume limits.

questions.stem: American depositary receipts are issued by
options: the foreign corporation whose shares they represent.
the SEC.
domestic branches of U.S. banks.
foreign stock exchanges.
questions.explanation: ADRs are receipts for foreign shares issued by domestic branches of U.S. banks, which hold the underlying shares, collect dividends, and convert them to dollars.
why: The foreign company issues the underlying shares, not the receipt.
The SEC regulates; it does not issue securities.
Exchanges trade ADRs; they do not issue them.

questions.stem: A client holding ADRs of a Japanese automaker would be subject to all of the following EXCEPT
options: currency risk.
market risk.
withholding of Japanese tax on dividends, creditable against U.S. tax.
preemptive rights on new issues of the automaker's shares.
questions.explanation: ADR holders receive dividends (in dollars, net of foreign withholding for which a U.S. credit is available) and sometimes votes, but never preemptive rights. Currency and market risk remain even though the ADR trades in dollars.
why: Dollar trading does not remove currency risk.
ADRs trade in the market and carry market risk.
The bank withholds foreign tax; the holder gets a U.S. credit.

questions.stem: An ADR of a European company trades at $40 on the NYSE. Over the next year the company's share price in euros is unchanged, but the euro falls 10% against the dollar. The ADR's dollar price would most likely
options: be unchanged, since ADRs trade in U.S. dollars.
decline, reflecting currency risk.
rise, because a weaker euro helps exporters.
decline only if the company cuts its dividend.
questions.explanation: The ADR represents shares valued in euros; when the euro weakens, those shares are worth fewer dollars. This is the currency risk ADR holders bear despite dollar trading.
why: Trading in dollars does not eliminate exposure to the underlying currency.
Any export benefit is speculative; the direct effect of a weaker euro is a lower dollar value.
Currency movement affects price independent of dividends.

questions.stem: A government unexpectedly announces it will nationalize all foreign-owned mining assets without compensation. Investors in that country's mining stocks have experienced
options: currency risk.
country risk.
exchange-control risk.
liquidity risk.
questions.explanation: Country risk is the composite of political and structural risks of a particular nation — including confiscatory policies toward profits and assets.
why: No exchange-rate movement is described.
Exchange controls restrict currency conversion or movement.
The loss comes from government action, not inability to sell.

questions.stem: Which characteristic is most associated with emerging markets rather than developed markets?
options: Low commission rates
Highly liquid markets with many market makers
Restrictions on foreign ownership and currency conversion
Transparent regulation comparable to the U.S.
questions.explanation: Emerging markets typically restrict foreign ownership and currency conversion, have thinner liquidity, higher costs, and weaker regulation; the other choices describe developed markets.
why: Emerging markets have high commission costs.
Emerging markets have questionable liquidity.
Emerging markets have lower regulatory standards and less transparency.

questions.front: Is a preferred stockholder an owner or a creditor?
questions.back: An owner. All stock — common and preferred — is equity. Only bondholders are creditors.
Annual dividend per share ÷ current market price. ($2 ÷ $60 = 3.33%)

questions.front: Is a stock dividend taxable when received?
questions.back: No. It lowers the cost basis per share; tax comes when the shares are sold. Total value is unchanged.

questions.front: Who has preemptive rights — common or preferred?
questions.back: Common stockholders. Preferred holders generally do not (and ADRs never do).

questions.front: Three reasons to own common stock / three risks
questions.back: Reasons: capital appreciation, dividend income, inflation hedge. Risks: market risk, business risk, low priority at dissolution.

questions.front: Payment order: bond interest, common dividend, preferred arrears, current preferred dividend
questions.back: Bond interest → preferred arrears + current preferred → common.

questions.front: Which preferred is least appropriate for an investor wanting fixed income?
questions.back: Adjustable-rate preferred — its dividend floats with benchmark rates (price stays stable, income does not).

questions.front: Most important factor when analyzing a preferred for an income investor
questions.back: The issuer's ability to keep paying the dividend. (Not par value, not voting power — preferred has no maturity and no vote.)

questions.front: NSO: what is taxed, when, and how?
questions.back: The bargain element (FMV − strike) at exercise, as ordinary income (wages, with payroll tax). Employer deducts the same amount.

questions.front: ISO holding periods for long-term capital gain
questions.back: At least 2 years after grant AND at least 1 year after exercise. Bargain element at exercise is an AMT preference item. Max 10-year exercise window.

questions.front: Restricted stock vs. control stock — the defining feature of each
questions.back: Restricted: how acquired (unregistered sale) → 6-month hold for all, volume limits for affiliates. Control: who owns it (10%+ holder, officer, director, same-home family) → volume limits always. Both sold via Rule 144 / Form 144 filed by the seller.

questions.front: ADR: issuer, currency, rights, key risk
questions.back: Issued by domestic branches of U.S. banks; trades and pays dividends in USD; dividends yes, votes sometimes, preemptive rights never; still has currency risk.

questions.front: Four risks unique to foreign investing
questions.back: Country risk, exchange controls, currency risk, withholding taxes and fees.

terms.def: Market price minus the option strike price at exercise; ordinary income for an NSO, an AMT preference item for an ISO.
Director, officer, 10%+ holder, or same-household family member; any stock they own is control stock with volume limits on resale.
Preferred whose skipped dividends accrue as arrears and must be paid before common dividends.
Unpaid past dividends owed on cumulative preferred stock.
SEC form filed by the seller of restricted or control stock under Rule 144.
A common stockholder's right to maintain proportionate ownership by buying new shares before the public.
The date by which one must be a stockholder of record to vote or receive a declared dividend.
Stock acquired in an unregistered (private placement) sale; generally a 6-month holding period before resale.
SEC-registered entity (often a bank) that reissues stock certificates to new owners.
American depositary receipt — a dollar-denominated receipt for foreign shares, issued by U.S. banks.
